question: Graph nozzle diameter versus airflow in SPICE, then fuel mass flow versus airflow, with regression and separate fuel comparisons.
scope: Plot SPICE nozzle diameter (mm), then fuel mass flow (mg/s), versus air speed (cm/s), comparing fuels separately. Separate fuel-flow comparisons by nozzle diameter. Include per-group regressions only where there are at least three distinct air speeds and variation in y. All axes are imposed settings: fits describe experimental-design associations, not causal burning responses. Nozzle diameter has only three levels; repeated flow stages share ignitions.

introduction: Nozzle diameter has its strongest linear association with air speed for propane, while fuel-flow associations differ by fuel and nozzle size. Propane and 75% Propylene have negative fuel-flow slopes at the 0.4064 mm nozzle but positive slopes at both larger nozzles. These regressions describe associations among imposed settings, not causal burning responses; nozzle diameter has only three levels, and repeated flow stages share ignitions.
conclusion: **These regressions describe experimental design, not causal fuel effects.** SPICE’s description specifies different nozzle diameter/co-flow configurations for studying jet diffusion flames [20090014827:p2:b1]. In Chart 1, ethylene, propane and 50% Propylene have positive diameter slopes whose supplied 95% intervals exclude zero; propylene and 75% Propylene do not show a resolved linear association. Three diameter levels make these lines summaries of setting allocation, not continuous nozzle responses. **Separating fuel flow by nozzle is essential:** propane and 75% Propylene switch from negative slopes in Chart 2 to positive slopes in Charts 3–4, while propylene stays positive throughout. Ethylene’s and 50% Propylene’s flow-slope intervals include zero at the smaller nozzles, but not at 1.6002 mm. Even the strongest flow fit, 75% Propylene at 1.6002 mm (R² = 0.590; n = 34), represents only 12 ignitions. OLS uncertainty is clustered by ignition because repeated stages are not independent; confidence bands concern fitted means, not individual predictions. Methane lacks fits: four records/four ignitions overall and two/two per smaller nozzle fail the supplied minimum of five each; fits also require three distinct air speeds and y variation. Missing pairs are omitted, not zero, and fits remain within observed ranges. As general physical reasoning, fuel flow sets mass supply, while nozzle area and coflow influence jet transport and mixing; these setting-only plots cannot demonstrate resulting combustion mechanisms.

evidence.text: Detailed Research Description: The Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment (SPICE) will continue the study of fundamental phenomena related to understanding the mechanisms controlling the stability and extinction of jet diffusion flames begun with the Laminar Soot Processes (LSP) on STS-94. SPICE will stabilize an enclosed laminar flame in a co-flowing oxidizer, measure the overall flame shape to validate the theoretical and numerical predictions, measure the flame stabilization heights, and measure the temperature field to verify flame structure predictions. SPICE will determine the laminar smoke point properties of non-buoyant jet diffusion flames (i.e., the properties of the largest laminar jet diffusion flames that do not emit soot) for several fuels under different nozzle diameter/co-flow velocity configurations. Luminous flame shape measurements would also be made to verify models of the flame shapes under co-flow conditions. The smoke point is a simple measurement that has been found useful to study the influence of flow and fuel properties on the sooting propensity of flames. This information would help support current understanding of soot processes in laminar flames and by analogy in turbulent flames of practical interest.
